justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a relatively stable near-term outlook with modest upward drift over time. At the one-day horizon, I anchored closely to the prevailing price level, assuming mean-reverting behavior dominates over such a short window and that no major catalysts were imminent. The slight upward bias in the one-week and one-month estimates reflects a mild positive drift assumption consistent with longer-run trend momentum, though the incremental increases are small enough to suggest I was not expecting a strong directional move — more of a sideways-to-slightly-higher drift rather than a breakout.

The confidence interval widths grow substantially as the horizon extends, which reflects the standard statistical reality that uncertainty compounds over time. At one day, the interval spans roughly 54 points, reflecting normal intraday and overnight volatility. By one month, it widens to about 272 points, incorporating not just cumulative volatility but also the possibility of regime shifts, macro data surprises, or sentiment changes that could meaningfully reprice the asset. The widths were calibrated using historical realized volatility scaled to each horizon, with some additional fat-tail allowance beyond what a purely Gaussian model would suggest.

Several specific risks could push outcomes outside my stated intervals. On the downside, a sharper-than-expected deterioration in macroeconomic data — such as a significant miss in employment or inflation figures — could trigger risk-off repositioning and push prices well below my lower bounds. A sudden tightening in financial conditions or a geopolitical shock could amplify this. On the upside, an unexpectedly dovish policy signal, strong earnings or fundamental data, or a short-squeeze dynamic could push prices above the upper bound, particularly at the one-month horizon where the tail risks are more pronounced.

It is also worth noting that my intervals, while reasonably wide, are still parametric estimates built on historical patterns that may not fully capture structural breaks or correlated tail events. Liquidity crises, flash crashes, or rapid sentiment reversals in correlated markets can produce moves that exceed even 90% confidence intervals, and this is a known limitation of any forward-looking probabilistic forecast anchored to recent historical volatility regimes.
